paragraphs: The paper develops a probabilistic method for grouping documents as they arrive. A central issue is that an incoming document may belong to an existing group or introduce a new topic. The model therefore needs to accommodate a growing collection of clusters while representing uncertainty about their contents.

A Dirichlet process prior supplies this flexibility: the number of clusters is not fixed in advance. A general English language model provides the base distribution used when generating new clusters. Existing cluster uncertainty is represented through a Bayesian Dirichlet-multinomial distribution. These components give the system a probabilistic account of both established groups and the possibility of something new.

The authors estimate the model's hyperparameters from historical documents using empirical Bayes. They apply the resulting model to novelty detection in Topic Detection and Tracking and compare it with existing approaches. The stated contribution is a framework that connects online clustering and novelty detection through explicit uncertainty modeling; the abstract does not report a comparative performance outcome.
neurips-2004-a-probabilistic-model-for-o.tldr: A Bayesian document-clustering model allows new topics to emerge while representing uncertainty about existing clusters.

paragraphs: This paper studies classification when examples occupy related positions, focusing on pixels arranged in an image. Treating each pixel as an independent example overlooks the surrounding label pattern. For image segmentation, the authors therefore use both measured pixel features and the configuration of labels in a local neighborhood.

Their Topographic Support Vector Machine incorporates this information through a topographic kernel. Because a pixel's classification depends on nearby labels, the method cannot simply assign every label independently. It instead seeks a collective assignment in which neighboring decisions are mutually consistent. This makes the spatial arrangement part of the classification problem itself.

The authors show that their self-consistent labeling solution is equivalent to a recurrent neural network. They also compare the method with a conventional support vector machine on cell image segmentation, without stating the outcome in the abstract. The conceptual contribution is a way to extend feature-based classification to settings where nearby objects' labels carry information about one another.
neurips-2004-a-topographic-support-vecto.tldr: A topographic support vector machine jointly labels image pixels using both their features and neighboring label configurations.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether spatial data structures developed for exact nearest-neighbor search can also support efficient approximate search. This matters for high-dimensional data, including perception problems, where finding nearby examples is an important computational task. The authors investigate metric trees as an alternative to Locality Sensitive Hashing, or LSH.

Their proposed tree permits overlap between branches: a data point can appear in both children of a parent node. They also introduce approximate search procedures for finding multiple nearby points in this structure. The authors argue that these trees should benefit from the same random-projection approximations used by LSH, with a simpler algorithm and potentially greater efficiency.

An empirical evaluation covers five large, high-dimensional datasets and reports accelerations of up to 31 times over LSH. The abstract reports an advantage across the range of approximation levels evaluated. These results support overlapping metric trees as a practical approximate-search approach in the tested settings; the largest reported acceleration is a maximum, not a speedup promised for every query or dataset.
neurips-2004-an-investigation-of-practic.tldr: Overlapping metric trees support approximate nearest-neighbor search and achieve up to 31-fold acceleration over LSH in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Coreference analysis asks whether different mentions or records refer to the same underlying entity. The paper introduces several conditional-probability models for this problem, with noun phrase coreference as the application. Its main concern is how to make identity decisions together while using a broad range of evidence from the input.

The models are undirected graphical models with relational dependencies. They therefore avoid assuming that every pairwise identity decision should be made independently. Decisions about different pairs can inform one another within a shared model. This is important because the task concerns relationships among mentions, rather than just a collection of isolated pair comparisons.

Their conditional formulation also accommodates many input features without requiring a generative account of the dependencies among those features. The authors relate this advantage to the distinction between conditional random fields and hidden Markov models. They report positive results on noun phrase coreference in two standard text datasets, supporting the usefulness of combining relational decisions with flexible input evidence.
neurips-2004-conditional-models-of-ident.tldr: Conditional relational models combine dependent identity decisions with varied input features and show positive results on noun phrase coreference.

paragraphs: The paper presents a method for recognizing object classes in cluttered images without first segmenting the objects. It represents each object as a flexible arrangement of parts. An interest operator identifies local image observations, and recognition involves determining how object parts could correspond to those observations.

For each class, a conditional random field models the probability of an assignment between parts and local features. The authors extend this framework with hidden variables and combine the separate class-conditioned models into one recognition system. Parameters are fitted by maximum likelihood, and the system selects the class that is most probable under the resulting model.

The main stated benefit is flexibility in how observed features relate to one another. Many generative approaches assume conditional independence among local observations, which the authors argue may be too restrictive for a considerable number of object classes. Their discriminative framework relaxes that assumption while retaining a structured representation of object parts. The contribution is this modeling capability, rather than a reported numerical recognition gain.
neurips-2004-conditional-random-fields-f.tldr: A part-based conditional random field recognizes objects in clutter while relaxing restrictive independence assumptions about local image features.

paragraphs: Amino acid profiles describe mutation probabilities at individual sequence positions, providing richer information than a single sequence of symbols. That richness makes profile comparisons expensive and their contents harder to visualize. The paper addresses both problems by replacing profiles with symbols drawn from a larger, learned alphabet.

Each symbol can represent a common profile rather than only an individual amino acid. The authors construct the alphabet using an extension of the information bottleneck method that incorporates constraints and prior information about class distributions. The aim is to retain useful information while producing a compact textual representation that supports simpler sequence comparisons.

The resulting alignments are reported to be nearly as accurate as full profile-to-profile alignments while taking almost as little computation as individual or consensus sequence alignments. As a scale illustration, the abstract estimates that all-pairs SwissProt alignment would take years with profiles but under three days with the discrete encoding. This makes the accuracy-versus-computation tradeoff concrete and suggests a broader practical reach for profile information.
neurips-2004-discrete-profile-alignment-.tldr: A learned alphabet compresses amino acid profiles into symbols, enabling much faster alignment with nearly the accuracy of full profile comparisons.

paragraphs: Tracking a hand from images is difficult because its joints allow many configurations and ambiguous measurements can support several plausible poses. This paper represents a three-dimensional hand with a graphical model whose connections capture joint constraints. It uses nonparametric belief propagation to exploit that structure without costly discretization.

A further difficulty arises when one part of the hand hides another. Joint constraints are naturally local, but these self-occlusions create more complicated dependencies in evidence based on color and edges. The authors introduce binary hidden variables for the occlusion state of each pixel, showing how this additional representation can recover a local structure.

The tracking algorithm infers these occlusion variables in a distributed manner and analytically averages over their possible states when estimating hand position. Occlusion uncertainty is therefore included in the position estimate rather than ignored. Simulations show that the method can refine inaccurate initial configurations and track motion through extended image sequences, supporting its use for structured tracking under ambiguous visual evidence.
neurips-2004-distributed-occlusion-reaso.tldr: A graphical hand tracker uses nonparametric belief propagation and hidden occlusion variables to estimate motion while accounting for self-occlusion.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a family of probabilistic models designed to make inference about hidden variables fast. Its starting point is a difficulty with directed models: although they have been successful, their causal organization can make it hard to compute the hidden-variable distribution after observing data.

The proposed exponential family harmoniums use two layers and an undirected formulation. Exponential family distributions provide the statistical building blocks, while the model's structure supports fast inference. Learning proceeds by minimizing contrastive divergence. The distinction between inference and learning matters here: the architecture addresses how hidden information is recovered, while a separate optimization procedure fits the model.

The authors study one member of this family as a probabilistic approach to latent semantic indexing, connecting the general modeling idea to document retrieval. Their experiments report good retrieval performance, and the model also supports searching with keywords. The stated result is therefore both architectural and practical: a model family with fast inference, together with an information-retrieval application that performs well in the reported experiments.
neurips-2004-exponential-family-harmoniu.tldr: Exponential family harmoniums offer fast hidden-variable inference and show useful performance for document retrieval and keyword search.

paragraphs: This paper extends a layered sprite model so that its layers can undergo affine transformations. The extension allows the system to infer an object's affine pose while learning its shape and appearance at the same time. The object representation and its placement in the image are therefore estimated together.

Learning uses an augmented variational inference procedure with two stages of search. It first searches globally over a discretized space of transformations, then refines the result through local optimization. Bottom-up image cues restrict the transformations considered, helping the procedure converge correctly. These cues guide the search within a model that jointly explains object appearance and pose.

The authors present results on several video sequences and describe an extension for tracking an object whose appearance changes over time. That extension matters because the representation being tracked need not remain visually fixed throughout a sequence. The contribution is a generative framework that brings affine localization, appearance learning, and tracking into a shared inference process.
neurips-2004-generative-affine-localisat.tldr: An extended layered sprite model jointly learns object appearance and shape while estimating affine pose and supporting video tracking.

paragraphs: A statistical language model predicts how likely a word is in a given context. The paper argues that explicitly enumerating contexts, as in common n-gram approaches, misses statistical regularities shared across them. It instead learns hierarchical, distributed context representations with the goal of improving word prediction.

Unsupervised linear and nonlinear dimensionality-reduction methods initialize these representations. They then serve as inputs to a hierarchical mixture of experts, with each expert supplying a probability distribution over words. This couples a learned representation of context with a structured prediction mechanism. The authors state that their architecture permits substantially larger vocabularies and training corpora than the neural probabilistic model that inspired the representations.

On a bigram task with a vocabulary of sixty thousand words and three million training sentences, the method consistently improves over class-based bigram models. This provides evidence that the representation and architecture are useful at the reported scale. The paper also discusses longer multiword contexts, while the concrete experimental finding described in the abstract concerns bigram prediction.
neurips-2004-hierarchical-distributed-re.tldr: Learned distributed context representations feed a hierarchical mixture of experts and improve large-scale bigram prediction over class-based models.

paragraphs: The paper brings together three questions: how neurons represent sensory information, how attention influences that information, and how perceptual decisions emerge. It proposes a hierarchical neural architecture that combines noisy sensory input with top-down attentional prior information through Bayesian integration. The resulting computation supports perceptual discrimination.

A central target is an observed interaction between stimulus features. Prior information about location can modulate processing of orientation even though the two features are independent. The model offers an explicit explanation for this effect within its combined treatment of sensory evidence and attention. This links a particular perceptual phenomenon to the architecture's inference process.

The intermediate representations also exhibit known physiological properties of visual cortical neurons. In addition, the model illustrates a possible reconciliation between cortical and neuromodulatory representations of uncertainty. These claims connect the computational account to both behavior and neural representation, while keeping the uncertainty proposal at the level of a possible explanation rather than an established biological mechanism.
neurips-2004-inference-attention-and-dec.tldr: A Bayesian neural hierarchy combines sensory noise and attentional priors to explain perceptual decisions and interactions between location and orientation.

paragraphs: This paper examines kernel principal component analysis as part of a classification system, concentrating on its regularization properties. Regularization concerns how a learning method controls the complexity of its fitted solution. The authors ask what role this dimensionality-reduction step plays when it is followed by a support vector machine.

They argue that this combination is somewhat redundant from a regularization perspective. To address that overlap, they propose the Kernel Projection Machine. Its design draws on an analogy with regression under a Gaussian white noise model. The motivation is to use the regularizing role of projection more directly within a classification algorithm.

Preliminary experiments report performance matching that of a support vector machine. This suggests that the proposed construction can be competitive in the settings examined, while the preliminary character of the evidence remains important. The paper's main contribution is the connection it draws between kernel projection and regularization, together with an algorithm designed around that connection.
neurips-2004-kernel-projection-machine-a.tldr: The Kernel Projection Machine addresses overlapping regularization in KPCA-plus-SVM classification and preliminarily matches SVM performance.

paragraphs: The task is to identify particular cars among images that all depict cars. A specific instance may have only one training image, leaving too little evidence to build a dedicated model for that car. The paper instead learns what makes images match by observing other members of the same class.

Training examples are image pairs labeled as matching or nonmatching. The learner looks for features that remain consistent across matching instances while distinguishing mismatches. Images are represented through patches, and the method models distributions of similarity measurements on those patches. This makes the learning problem about the usefulness of local comparisons for identity.

An algorithm then selects informative patches using a mutual information criterion. The authors report good identification performance on their challenging car-image dataset after comparing only a few selected patches. The result supports the idea that experience with a class can guide instance matching when examples of a particular instance are scarce, and that carefully chosen local evidence can be sufficient for useful performance in this setting.
neurips-2004-learning-hyper-features-for.tldr: Learning from matching and nonmatching car images identifies a few informative patches that support instance recognition with scarce examples.

paragraphs: The paper uses machine learning to investigate human judgments of gender from face images. It combines human classification data with psychophysical discrimination experiments. The purpose is to connect a fitted classifier's decision rule to the visual changes that influence people's perception in this task.

The authors first reduce the face images with principal component analysis and then train several linear classifiers, including support vector machines, relevance vector machines, Fisher linear discriminants, and prototype classifiers. Because both stages are linear, the complete decision rule can be visualized as a decision image. This image corresponds to the direction perpendicular to the classifier's separating boundary.

For the support vector and relevance vector classifiers, which closely mimic human classifications, the authors predict the fastest perceived transition from female to male appearance along that perpendicular direction. A psychophysical experiment using the decision images is consistent with this prediction. The finding supports the use of interpretable classifier directions to formulate and test hypotheses about visual judgments.
neurips-2004-machine-learning-applied-to.tldr: Visualized linear classifiers generate predictions about perceived gender transitions in faces that are consistent with a psychophysical experiment.

paragraphs: A document can concern several topics at once. This paper treats the complete set of relevant topics as its label and asks how to predict that set. Its motivation is that a word can strongly indicate a particular topic combination without being especially useful for predicting either topic separately.

Maximal Margin Labeling treats every possible topic set as a distinct class, turning the task into multiclass classification. This makes features associated with combinations directly relevant to the decision. However, the many possible combinations create sparse training data. The method addresses that difficulty by combining prior knowledge about label prototypes with a maximal-margin learning criterion.

Experiments on web pages with multiple topics show the method outperforming existing learning algorithms, including support vector machines. The result supports learning complete topic combinations in the evaluated setting. Its significance is that useful document evidence can belong to the intersection of topics, and a classifier organized around whole labels can use that evidence while drawing on prior structure to address sparsity.
neurips-2004-maximal-margin-labeling-for.tldr: Maximal Margin Labeling learns whole topic combinations and uses label-prototype knowledge to address sparse data, outperforming comparison methods on multi-topic web pages.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to place data in a low-dimensional space when several kinds of similarity information are available. Its central idea is that different relationships can emphasize different aspects of the same data. A common underlying representation can therefore support several distinct views of similarity.

The method gives each relation its own weighting of the dimensions in a shared latent space. These weighted representations can overlap, so different relationships need not rely on entirely separate dimensions. When there is only one similarity relation based on Euclidean distances between input points, the method reduces to ordinary dimensionality reduction.

Additional information about the full dataset or just some of its members can guide the embedding and potentially improve it. This makes the approach a form of semi-supervised dimensionality reduction: the low-dimensional representation can reflect more than the original distances alone. The authors demonstrate its potential usefulness on simple examples, providing illustrative support for integrating multiple relationships without claiming broad empirical validation.
neurips-2004-multiple-relational-embeddi.tldr: Multiple similarity relations shape a shared low-dimensional embedding through relation-specific weights on its dimensions.

paragraphs: The paper proposes standards for learning in multi-agent systems, applying most directly to repeated games evaluated by average reward. The standards distinguish performance against a specified opponent class, performance against other opponents, and performance when the algorithm plays against another copy of itself. They also require good average rewards to be reached quickly.

Against the specified class, payoff should approach that of the best response. Against other opponents, it should at least approach the security-level payoff, the maximin benchmark. Subject to those requirements, self-play should achieve a nearly optimal payoff. The authors argue that this combination is more stringent and better justified than earlier criteria.

They introduce an algorithm and show that it satisfies the criteria when the specified class consists of stationary opponents. A separate empirical evaluation on a comprehensive game-theoretic test suite finds that it outperforms previous learning algorithms almost universally. The theoretical statement is tied to that opponent class, while the experiments provide additional evidence about comparative performance across the tested games.
neurips-2004-new-criteria-and-a-new-algo.tldr: New multi-agent learning criteria balance best responses, security, and self-play, and an algorithm meets them for stationary opponents with strong empirical results.

paragraphs: The paper argues that a broad class of local manifold-learning methods faces a curse of dimensionality governed by the underlying manifold's dimension. The argument concerns methods that are essentially local and can be expressed as kernel learning. It motivates looking beyond separate neighborhood-based estimates of the data's structure.

The proposed direction is to learn structure shared by tangent planes at different locations. A tangent plane describes the local directions along which a manifold varies. Sharing information across these planes could let a model predict local geometry at locations distant from its training examples. The authors propose a learning criterion and experiment with a function that predicts tangent planes.

In experiments involving rotations of handwritten character images, the method generalizes far from training data where a local nonparametric method fails. This supports the value of shared, nonlocal structure in that setting. The evidence connects a specific generalization result to the paper's broader argument, without establishing that every local method fails or every nonlocal method succeeds.
neurips-2004-non-local-manifold-tangent-.tldr: Learning shared structure across manifold tangent planes enables distant generalization in character-rotation experiments where a local method fails.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a conceptual problem in many one-class outlier detectors: they require the expected proportion of outliers to be specified beforehand. The authors seek a way to judge atypical objects through a fitted statistical model rather than relying on that advance specification.

Their method connects kernelized one-class classification to Gaussian density estimation in the feature space induced by the kernel. Once this relationship is established, an object's atypicality can be assessed by quantifying its departure from the Gaussian model. This gives the classification procedure a density-based interpretation and a corresponding basis for detecting unusual observations.

For radial basis function kernels, the authors show that the Gaussian construction is sufficiently expressive to yield an asymptotically unbiased estimate of the true density. The asymptotic qualification matters: the statement concerns limiting behavior, rather than exact accuracy for every finite dataset. To select the model's free parameters, they apply a cross-validated likelihood criterion. Together, these elements address both the interpretation of outliers and the choice of model settings.
neurips-2004-outlier-detection-with-one-.tldr: A density-based interpretation of kernel one-class classification detects atypical objects without prespecifying their expected fraction.

paragraphs: Parametric Embedding visualizes the probabilities a model assigns to classes by placing both objects and classes in a shared low-dimensional space. Its input is a class-posterior vector for each object. The goal is to preserve these probability relationships so the display reveals how the model associates objects with classes.

The embedding minimizes a sum of Kullback-Leibler divergences under an explicit assumption: samples in the display space follow a Gaussian mixture whose components have equal covariances. Thus, the visualization is fitted to posterior structure through a particular probabilistic model. Its computational cost scales with the number of objects multiplied by the number of classes, offering an advantage over conventional methods based on pairwise object relationships.

The authors demonstrate supervised web-page categorization, semi-supervised digit categorization, and relationships between words and latent topics from Latent Dirichlet Allocation. These examples illustrate how the same visualization method can expose model behavior across different learning settings. The useful information being displayed is the pattern of class probabilities, rather than only similarities between original data points.
neurips-2004-parametric-embedding-for-cl.tldr: Parametric Embedding jointly visualizes objects and classes by preserving class-probability structure under an equal-covariance Gaussian mixture assumption.

paragraphs: Schema learning builds probabilistic models of action effects from experience. The paper extends this approach for situations where observations do not fully reveal the current state. In such settings, maintaining useful hidden-state information can make predictions more accurate than relying on current sensor readings alone.

The extensions allow arbitrary discrete-valued sensors, revise the learning criteria for partially observable Markov decision process domains, and use schema predictions to maintain hidden state more effectively. These changes broaden the observations the mechanism can handle and improve how its learned predictions contribute to subsequent prediction. The work centers on constructing predictive action models from experience.

Experiments show large improvements over the original mechanism in several rewardless partially observable domains and very low prediction error on a difficult speech-modeling task. Comparisons with predictive state representations find approximately equal accuracy for next-step action effects. The authors present these results as a foundation for integrated learning and planning, with the reported evidence specifically establishing predictive capabilities rather than a completed planning system.
neurips-2004-schema-learning-experience-.tldr: Extensions to schema learning improve hidden-state prediction and action models in partially observable tasks, with strong reported prediction results.

paragraphs: The paper tackles reconstruction of an underwater image distorted by waves at the surface. It starts with a large amount of video showing the distorted image and formulates recovery locally: at each spatial position, the task is to find the corresponding undistorted image patch.

The authors recast this reconstruction as a manifold-learning problem. In their formulation, the changing distorted observations have a manifold whose center represents the undistorted patch. Recovering the image therefore depends on locating that center. This connects the physical reconstruction task to estimating the geometry of a collection of observed patches.

To compute the center, the paper introduces a method for estimating global distances on the manifold. It uses convex flow computations to obtain robustness and is stated to solve the leakage problem in recent manifold-embedding techniques. The contribution links a new geometric distance calculation to a concrete reconstruction objective: using many wave-distorted observations to recover the undistorted image patch at each location.
neurips-2004-seeing-through-water-1dc857.tldr: Wave-distorted underwater video is reconstructed through manifold centers, using a new global-distance method based on convex flow computations.

paragraphs: This paper asks what a single model neuron can learn when two forms of adaptation operate together. Intrinsic plasticity changes the neuron's own response properties, while synaptic plasticity changes its connections to incoming signals. The study examines their combined computational effect within an individual neuron model.

The authors propose an intrinsic-plasticity mechanism for a neuron with continuous activation. It uses low-order moments, or compact statistical summaries, of the neuron's firing-rate distribution. Its objective is to enforce sparse activity, concentrating the neuron's responses into a distribution in which strong activation is selective. The learning target therefore concerns the pattern of activity across inputs.

When this mechanism is combined with Hebbian learning at the synapses, the neuron is shown to discover sparse directions in its input. The result connects control of the neuron's activity distribution with the input structure learned by its connections. Its significance is the demonstrated cooperation between two adaptive mechanisms in the model, rather than a claim that synaptic learning alone produces the same outcome.
neurips-2004-synergies-between-intrinsic.tldr: An intrinsic-plasticity rule that promotes sparse activity works with Hebbian synaptic learning to discover sparse input directions in a model neuron.

paragraphs: The paper combines face detection and facial pose estimation in a single real-time method. Rather than treating the presence of a face and its pose as unrelated predictions, it trains a convolutional network around a shared geometric representation. Face images are mapped onto a manifold organized by pose, while non-face images are mapped far away.

Training uses a loss involving the image, its pose, and its face-or-non-face label. The representation therefore has to capture variation among faces while also separating faces from other images. This design connects the two tasks directly: pose organizes the face representation, and detection distinguishes that representation from non-face content.

One system configuration is evaluated on three standard datasets covering frontal faces, rotated faces, and profiles. On each, its performance is comparable to earlier multi-view detectors restricted to one form of pose variation. Experiments also show that joint training improves accuracy on both detection and pose estimation. These findings support the benefit of sharing a representation across the two tasks in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2004-synergistic-face-detection-.tldr: A shared pose-organized face representation enables real-time detection and pose estimation, with joint training improving both tasks experimentally.

paragraphs: This paper accelerates object detection by focusing on quickly rejecting image patches before they reach a full classifier. It demonstrates the idea with faces and presents the rejection stage as preprocessing for methods such as neural networks, Bayes classifiers, and support vector machines. The aim is to reduce how many patches require expensive classification.

The method groups pixels into image regions according to how similarly they behave across a collection of face images. Relationships between regional means and variances then form a cascade of rejection rules. The feature shapes are learned from data, are inexpensive to compute, and create a space small enough to search exhaustively for the best features.

The reported cascade rejects more than 99.8 percent of image patches, leaving only a small fraction for the full classifier. Training takes much less than an hour on a standard PC. These findings concern the efficiency of the learned filtering stage: the rejection percentage describes the amount of candidate processing removed, rather than a face-detection accuracy score.
neurips-2004-the-power-of-feature-cluste.tldr: Learned image-segment features form a cheap rejection cascade that filters over 99.8 percent of patches before full classification.
